source.title: Deep Learning is Not So Mysterious or Different

record.tranche_reason: Presents adapted CIFAR noisy-label results and a width sweep with test loss and effective dimensionality; these bear on memorization with generalization, wider models, and measured properties tracking generalization.
record.gate_note: Most other examples are conceptual or cited prior work; they are not recorded as study results. Figure 1(d)-(f) is adapted from earlier work, and the text describes the results. No exact plotted values are stated in the text.
record.test_reason: The neural-network experiments in R2–R4 are adapted from prior studies, rather than this study's own results. Its own polynomial and linear-model demonstrations do not test the specified neural-network versions. Its argument disputes these phenomena's supposed mystery and uniqueness, rather than the empirical claims V1–V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the author argues that benign overfitting, overparameterization, and double descent are understandable through soft inductive biases and established PAC-Bayes and countable-hypothesis frameworks, and occur outside deep learning.
record.recipe_differences: Presents adapted noisy-label CIFAR-10 results and a width sweep rather than testing the original claim versions' specified model recipes and measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The noisy-label results steadily degrade as the number of altered labels increases; in the ResNet-18 width sweep test loss rises in the transition regime and falls in the interpolation regime.

fits_no_version.finding: An RBF Gaussian process perfectly fits altered CIFAR-10 labels while test performance deteriorates with increasing corruption; reproduced from earlier work.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Memorization capacity and useful generalization can coexist in Gaussian processes.

fits_no_version.finding: Adapted ResNet results associate decreasing Hessian effective dimensionality with improving test loss during the second descent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hessian effective dimensionality can track test loss across overparameterized widths.

fits_no_version.finding: The study demonstrates structured-data fitting and noise fitting with regularized polynomials, and double descent with a linear random-feature model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Analogues of benign overfitting and double descent occur outside neural networks.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning; Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: Results relevant to V1 are adapted from prior work; the text gives qualitative descriptions rather than exact plotted values, and does not state chance-level accuracy. The width sweep is also adapted from prior work.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying results were identified. Other findings discussed in the text are conceptual or attributed to cited work.

untested.parts: No independent neural-network experiment comparing natural and fixed random labels, training fit, and held-out accuracy.
No independent neural-network width sweep testing held-out error beyond zero training error.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-classification comparison.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparison under specified tuning budgets.
No batch-size comparison with fixed epoch budgets or adapted training recipes.
No dropout intervention measuring held-out error.
No magnitude-aware sharpness versus generalization-gap evaluation or ranking comparison.
No removal and retraining experiment comparing memorized examples with random removals.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the extracted verdicts. The transition-region increase in test loss does not independently limit V2's claim about widths beyond interpolation. Failure to measure magnitude-aware sharpness does not limit V7. Neither the paper's title nor its criticism of earlier interpretations challenges V1's empirical finding.

versions.untested_parts: The text reports CIFAR-10 noisy-label results for a Gaussian process and ResNet, not the specified Inception, AlexNet, or MLP settings; the text does not state held-out accuracy or chance-level accuracy.
The width sweep uses ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100, not one-hidden-layer ReLU networks on MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10; no explicit-regularization setting is stated.
The width sweep reports effective dimensionality of the Hessian, but does not compare magnitude-aware sharpness or the tested norm- and margin-based measures specified in the version.

rows.subject: Gaussian process (GP) with an RBF kernel
rows.operation_detail: Fit CIFAR-10 with increasing numbers of altered labels.
rows.measure: Training error and generalization on CIFAR-10 with altered labels
rows.value: No training error; generalization is reasonable and steadily degrades with increasing numbers of altered labels.
rows.note: The paper says this reproduces the mixed noisy-label experiment; it gives no exact test accuracy or chance-level comparison.
rows.check: A Gaussian process is outside V1's neural-network scope. This is also an adapted result from Wilson & Izmailov (2020), not an independent result of this study.

rows.subject: ResNet (PreResNet-20 in Appendix D)
rows.operation_detail: Fit CIFAR-10 with increasing numbers of altered labels.
rows.measure: Training error and generalization on CIFAR-10 with altered labels
rows.value: No training error; generalization is reasonable and steadily degrades with increasing numbers of altered labels.
rows.note: The results are adapted from Wilson & Izmailov (2020); exact test accuracy and chance-level comparison are not stated.
rows.check: Adapted from Wilson & Izmailov (2020); exclude as this study's own result. The qualitative description supports coexistence of fitting and generalization but does not establish V1's full natural-label versus fully random-label accuracy comparison. Missing endpoint information does not establish a partial effect.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Increase layer width and measure train loss and test loss.
rows.value: In the interpolation regime, test loss decreases with increases in parameters; all models achieve a perfect fit to the data.
rows.note: Figure adapted from Maddox et al. (2020). The text describes the trend but supplies no numeric values.
rows.check: Adapted from Maddox et al. (2020); exclude as this study's own result. The reported second-descent trend is observed, not partial merely because the architecture and dataset differ. The measure is cross-entropy loss rather than classification error. Perfect fitting applies to the second-descent models, not every width in the sweep.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Measure effective dimensionality of the Hessian alongside train and test loss across widths.
rows.measure: Effective dimensionality of the Hessian of the trained parameters
rows.value: Effective dimensionality decreases as parameters continue to increase in the second descent, while generalization improves.
rows.note: The text presents this as an explanatory trend, not a magnitude-aware sharpness comparison; no numeric values are stated.
rows.check: Hessian effective dimensionality is not V7's magnitude-scaled perturbation measure, and this row does not compare generalization-gap rankings against norm and margin measures. The result is also adapted from Maddox et al. (2020).

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
